questions.q: State the theorem about lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle. Draw a labelled diagram showing the circle, centre, external point, points of contact, and the two tangent segments.
questions.a: The theorem states: "The lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal." In the diagram, if P is the external point, A and B are points of contact, and O is the centre, then PA = PB. A wrong answer where the student draws the external point inside the circle or draws secants instead of tangents reveals confusion between "external point" (outside the circle) and "point on the circle" — from c10_math_cbse_10_004 and c10_math_cbse_10_005, only external points have two equal tangents; points on the circle have exactly one tangent of length zero from that point.

questions.q: In the proof of the theorem, we use RHS congruence of triangles OAP and OBP. Explain why the condition ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° is essential and which prior theorem gives us this right angle.
questions.a: The right angles come from the theorem "Tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact" (c10_math_cbse_10_003). This is essential because RHS congruence specifically requires a right angle, the hypotenuse, and one side. Without the 90° angles, we would only have two sides (OA = OB radii, OP common) which gives SSA — not a valid congruence criterion. A student who says "we use SAS with the included angle" reveals they don't recognise that the angle between OA and OP is not known to be equal to the angle between OB and OP; the right angles are at A and B, not at O.

questions.q: From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle of radius 6 cm. If OP = 10 cm, find the length of each tangent. Show all steps.
questions.a:
Given: OA = 6 cm (radius), OP = 10 cm, ∠OAP = 90°.
In right triangle OAP, by Pythagoras theorem: OP² = OA² + AP²
10² = 6² + AP² → 100 = 36 + AP² → AP² = 64 → AP = 8 cm.
Since PA = PB (theorem), each tangent length = 8 cm.
A wrong answer of AP = 10 cm (using OP as a leg) or AP = 4 cm (subtracting radii) reveals the student cannot identify the right triangle or misapplies Pythagoras theorem. This connects to Class 8 Pythagoras theorem (c8_math_ch9_5, c8_math_ch9_8) and Class 9 distance formula (c9_math_ch1_4).

questions.q: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from point P to a circle with centre O. If ∠APB = 70°, find ∠AOB. Explain the relationship between ∠APB and ∠AOB in general.
questions.a:
In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (tangent ⟂ radius). Sum of angles = 360°.
∠AOB + 90° + 90° + 70° = 360° → ∠AOB = 110°.
General relationship: ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180° (supplementary).
A student who answers ∠AOB = 70° (thinking they are equal) or ∠AOB = 140° (doubling) reveals they don't use the quadrilateral angle sum property or forget the two right angles. This tests synthesis of tangent perpendicular property (c10_math_cbse_10_003), quadrilateral angle sum (Class 8 c8_math_ch4_12), and the equal tangent theorem.

questions.q: A student solves: "PA and PB are tangents from P to circle with centre O. PA = 5 cm. Find PB." The student writes: "PA = PB = 5 cm because tangents from external point are equal." Is this solution complete for full marks in CBSE board exam? Justify.
questions.a: No, the solution is incomplete for full marks. CBSE marking scheme requires: (1) Statement of the theorem, (2) A labelled diagram, (3) The given data (PA = 5 cm), (4) The conclusion PB = 5 cm with reason "Lengths of tangents from an external point are equal." Just writing the answer without the theorem statement and diagram loses 1-2 marks. A student who thinks the answer alone suffices reveals misunderstanding of board exam expectations — they must show the logical chain: Given → Theorem → Conclusion.

questions.q: Create a real-world problem where a person needs to use the equal tangent lengths property. The problem should involve finding an unknown distance and must include a diagram description.
questions.a:
Example: "A circular pond of radius 4 m has a centre O. Two straight walkways are built from a gate P outside the pond, touching the pond at A and B. If the gate is 10 m from the centre of the pond, find the length of each walkway. Also find the distance between the two touching points A and B along the straight line AB."
A good answer sets up right triangle OAP, uses Pythagoras to get PA = PB = √(10² - 4²) = √84 ≈ 9.17 m, then uses the fact that OP bisects ∠APB and AB to find AB using trigonometry or area method. A poor answer that cannot set up the right triangle or forgets PA = PB reveals inability to translate the geometric property into a practical measurement scenario.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: If two tangents are drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O, touching the circle at points A and B ______, then the lengths of the tangent segments PA and PB are equal.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are designing a ______ garden with a fountain at the centre.
What is If two tangents? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: If two tangents are drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O, touching the circle at points A and B respectively, then the lengths of the tangent segments PA and PB are equal.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This holds because triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by RHS criterion (OA = OB = radii, OP = common hypotenuse, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = ______°).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about If two tangents?
questions.a: Students often confuse "equal tangents from an external point" with "equal tangents from a point on the circle" — they think a point on the circle also has two equal tangents.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can prove the theorem using RHS congruence of right triangles, apply it to find unknown tangent lengths in geometric figures, and use it to solve problems involving circumscribed triangles and quadrilaterals where tangent segments from vertices are equal.
